name: actinic reticuloid
aliases: photosensitivity dermatitis and actinic reticuloid syndrome

clinicalPearls: Represents the most severe end of the chronic actinic dermatitis spectrum, typically in older men with intensely pruritic, thickened, lichenified and infiltrated plaques on sun-exposed skin.
The action spectrum is characteristically broad, with abnormal reactivity extending across UVB, UVA and often visible light, so ordinary sunscreens give incomplete protection.
Phototesting shows a markedly reduced minimal erythema dose across multiple wavebands, which is central to confirming the diagnosis.

Histology may closely mimic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (a pseudolymphomatous pattern with atypical lymphocytes), but the dermal infiltrate is usually CD8 predominant rather than the CD4 predominance of true lymphoma.

Coexisting allergic contact or photocontact sensitivity is common, particularly to sesquiterpene lactones (Compositae plants), fragrances and sunscreens, so patch and photopatch testing are essential.
Severe disease may generalise to involve covered skin and progress to erythroderma with leonine facial thickening.
Strict photoprotection, including from visible light and behind window glass, combined with avoidance of identified contact allergens, is the cornerstone of management.
The condition mainly affects skin of the head, neck and dorsal hands, with a sharp cut-off at clothing lines when photo-driven.
reference.pathophysiology: Actinic reticuloid is understood as a persistent, delayed-type (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity response in which ultraviolet, and sometimes visible, radiation converts an endogenous cutaneous molecule into a photo-induced antigen. Repeated antigen presentation drives a chronic dermal T-lymphocyte infiltrate that produces the dense, lichenified plaques and the pseudolymphomatous histological appearance. Many patients have concurrent contact or photocontact allergy, which appears to prime or perpetuate the reaction, and abnormal reactivity persists long after the initiating exposure, explaining the chronic, self-sustaining course.
additionalInvestigations: Monochromator phototesting to define the action spectrum and minimal erythema dose
Patch testing and photopatch testing for coexisting contact and photocontact allergy
Skin biopsy with assessment of infiltrate and immunophenotype (CD4/CD8 ratio)
Peripheral blood flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies to exclude lymphoma when atypia is marked
Autoimmune serology (antinuclear and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies) to exclude lupus
Urinary and erythrocyte porphyrin studies to exclude porphyria
redFlags: Progression to erythroderma with systemic upset and temperature dysregulation
Persistent lymphadenopathy or circulating atypical lymphocytes raising concern for lymphoma
Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating plaques suggesting transformation
Failure to improve despite rigorous photoprotection and allergen avoidance
reference.prognosis: The condition tends to be chronic and can persist for many years, but a substantial proportion of patients improve or remit with strict photoprotection and avoidance of identified allergens. Rarely, severe refractory disease requires systemic immunosuppression.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the pseudolymphomatous histology as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, leading to inappropriate aggressive therapy.
Overlooking coexisting contact or photocontact allergy, which perpetuates the eruption.
Relying on standard UVB sunscreens that fail to block the visible and UVA wavelengths driving the disease.
Attributing generalised involvement to a primary lymphoma rather than to spread of photosensitive dermatitis onto covered skin.
